title: thoughts are misunderstood
content:
As I sit, feeling intensely, a thought appears out of nowhere.

The thought wants to capture the feeling. It wants to give it a name, hold it still and place it aboard one of the many boats of impermanence. Perhaps, through memory or language, some part of the feeling can be carried forward.

In the odd case that the thought succeeds, another thought arrives bearing the flag of surprise. It pokes the first thought until it bends and changes. Soon, I am no longer feeling what I originally felt. I am thinking about a thought I had about a feeling.

The feeling itself was pristine.

Anger, love, jealousy, gratitude, greed, lust, devotion - before we divide them into desirable and undesirable, each of them is energy. Each takes hold of life and announces: *Something matters here.*

Thought is something else. It is a representation of that energy, a condensed and almost flat unidimensional version of reality.

The way I see it, a thought is like a strand of hair appearing above the skin. We see the hair and imagine that we have seen the thing. But beneath it is the follicle, the skin, blood, nerves and an entire living mechanism operating invisibly. The visible strand is only what has managed to reach the surface.

Thought is that strand.

Feeling is the hidden life beneath it.

This does not make thought useless. A feeling without thought may be alive but incommunicable. Thought gives it an outline. It allows us to remember, speak, write and offer some part of our inner life to the outside world.

It allows survival.

The mistake begins when we confuse the outline for the whole.

> A person who can feel intensely is one whom life trusts.

There is also a strange connection between us and the world. At the level of thought, the separation is crystal clear: this is me, and the world is not me. I am here; the tree, the street and the stranger are there.

But feeling does not always obey this boundary.

On a bright day, when you are particularly open and happy, take a walk through a nearby park or a bustling street. There may be a peculiar receptivity in the air—a sense of grace, intimacy and love. It can almost feel as though everything happening around you is happening around you, for you. The trees appear more alive. A stranger’s laughter enters you. Even the movement of traffic seems to belong to the same event as your breathing.

As a thought, this is insidious.

Try telling your friends or family that everything happens for you and that you are special. Depending on your delivery, you may be labelled a lunatic or an enlightened master. In either case, do not think yourself into becoming one. If you were truly a lunatic or an enlightened being, the declaration would probably be rarer—and certainly not an act of bragging.

But as a feeling, the experience is neither lunacy nor enlightenment. It is simply a temporary dissolution of distance. Nothing has objectively become yours, yet nothing feels entirely separate from you.

This is exactly where thought and feeling diverge.

Consider the ancient epics—the *Ramayana*, the *Mahabharata*. They speak of gods, demons, humans, war, love, duty, betrayal and ultimate reality. A hierarchy naturally presents itself. Thought immediately begins its work: Who represents what? What power does this god possess? What is the author trying to say? Is this historical, symbolic, political or metaphysical?

Thought arrives with a chisel. It dissects the story into elemental pieces and scrapes every possible meaning out of them.

A child listening to the same story does something entirely different.

The child sees thunder striking armour. He sees a warrior standing alone on a battlefield. He hears the conch. He watches cows grazing in a field while a flute plays beneath a tree.

Mann, is it beautiful.

The child has not understood less. Perhaps, for that moment, the child has entered more.

Seen only through thought, a story can dry up. Touched by feeling, it opens into a world.

This may be why the old stories lasted. They did not survive merely because their propositions were preserved. They survived because generation after generation could become afraid, devoted, furious, tender and astonished through them.

A story does not preserve a feeling by keeping it unchanged. It preserves the possibility that the feeling may be born again.

Thought tries to preserve feeling by fixing it.

Story preserves feeling by releasing it.

There are also people who seem to know through their being what others arrive at through years of reasoning. They cannot always explain what they know. Ask them for a theory and they may offer only a sentence: “Yes, I know.”

For someone who has travelled through logic, doubt and language to reach that understanding, such a response can be unsettling.

*How do you know? Where is the reasoning? Show me the path you took.*

But perhaps there was no path of that kind.

A dancer may know balance without possessing the language of mechanics. A mother may recognise pain before it is spoken. A person may inhabit tenderness without ever developing a philosophy of love.

Some of us arrive at life through thought. Others seem already to be standing where thought is trying to go.

They may know more than they can say.

We may say more than we can live.

> Neither way of knowing is complete by itself. Thought can help embodied knowledge become conscious and communicable. Embodied knowledge can rescue thought from becoming an elaborate substitute for life.

Before we go and declare feeling the ultimate way of being, let us admit that it has its own difficulty: momentum.

Thought is quick. It can move from work to love, from love to prayer and from prayer to an email in a matter of seconds. Modern life is built around this ability. We close one window and open another. We move between roles, tasks and conversations, expecting the rest of ourselves to follow.

The heart does not move like that.

The heart moves through absorption. Whatever it feels deeply becomes, for a while, the whole horizon.

The clock may announce that it is time to change contexts. The heart has no obligation to agree.

Remember goodbyes?

This is where things get tricky. Work asks something of the heart. Love asks something else. The spiritual path asks for something else altogether. Thought can hold all three as important, but the heart may give itself so completely to one that the others disappear from view.

Not because they no longer matter.

They are simply not being felt.

It would be easy to call this inefficiency, but that misses something. The problem may not be the heart’s absorption. The problem may be our demand that it shift at the speed of thought.

And yet, how does one carry out a life like this?

Perhaps there is a way to romance these various worlds together without being consumed by any one of them. It reminds me of the Maharaas! Krishna fully present to each, the dance somehow whole without intimacy being divided.

Intriguing.

I do not yet know what that means for an ordinary human life. Today’s exploration ends there.
